tutorial_example_entry.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Derive the Fourier-domain output relation $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ by applying the Fourier transform to the LTI convolution equation and identifying $H(j\omega)$ as the transform of the impulse response.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Introduction to Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output

blocks.text: For one continuous-time LTI system, the output is determined by the impulse response $h(t)$ and the input $x(t)$. In this lesson, we start from the standard time-domain description of that output, not from a new system model.

That convolution equation is the starting point for the frequency-domain derivation. The next steps will apply the Fourier transform to both sides and use the convolution theorem to turn the time-domain convolution into a product.

Here $H(j\omega)$ names the Fourier transform of $h(t)$. So the output spectrum is the input spectrum $X(j\omega)$ multiplied by the system frequency response, and the later steps will show that identification in detail.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Writing the LTI Output as a Convolution

example_content.example_prompt: Given an LTI system with input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$, write the output $y(t)$ as a convolution integral.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the standard LTI setup: input $x(t)$, impulse response $h(t)$, and output $y(t)$. For an LTI system, the output is written as the convolution of the input with the impulse response.
Expand that convolution into its integral form so the time-domain relation is explicit. Keep the roles of $x(t)$, $h(t)$, and $y(t)$ distinct.

This is the time-domain starting point for the frequency-domain derivation. The next step will transform this same equation; here the only new move is writing the LTI output in standard convolution form.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Applying the Fourier Transform to the Convolution Equation

example_content.example_prompt: Starting from $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, apply the Fourier transform to both sides and write the transformed relation.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the convolution equation from the previous step. Apply the Fourier transform to both sides of that equation, and name the transformed output spectrum $Y(j\omega)$ without changing the system model.
Keep the right-hand side symbolic at this stage; the convolution theorem will simplify it in the next step. The only new move here is moving the LTI output equation into Fourier form.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Using the Convolution Theorem on the Output Spectrum

example_content.example_prompt: Take the transformed convolution relation from the previous step and simplify it using the convolution theorem.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the transformed convolution relation from the previous step. Apply the convolution theorem to replace the transformed convolution with the product of the two individual transforms, while keeping the same frequency variable $j\omega$.

This is the frequency-domain product form of the output relation. The only new move here is using the convolution theorem to replace the transformed convolution with a product of spectra, without yet renaming the transform of $h(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output

example_content.example_prompt: Given the impulse response $h(t)$, identify its Fourier transform $H(j\omega)$ and substitute it into the output relation.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the transform of the impulse response from the previous step. Name that transform as $H(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$, then substitute it into the frequency-domain product so the system term is written with standard notation.
This is the frequency-response notation for the LTI system. The input spectrum stays $X(j\omega)$, the output spectrum stays $Y(j\omega)$, and the system contribution is now isolated as $H(j\omega)$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output

example_content.example_prompt: Starting from the convolution equation and the definition of $H(j\omega)$, derive the final relation $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the full derivation from the time-domain LTI model to the frequency-domain output formula. Start with the convolution expression, transform both sides, use the convolution theorem, and then replace $\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$ with $H(j\omega)$.
This completes the lesson's core move. The output spectrum is the input spectrum multiplied by the system frequency response, so the final relation is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

question_entry.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
question_entry.lesson_core_move: Derive the Fourier-domain output relation $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ by applying the Fourier transform to the LTI convolution equation and identifying $H(j\omega)$ as the transform of the impulse response.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Writing the LTI Output as a Convolution

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression correctly writes the output $y(t)$ of an LTI system with input $u(t)$ and impulse response $g(t)$ in convolution notation?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: An LTI system output is written as the input convolved with the impulse response, so $y(t)=u(t)*g(t)$ is the correct symbolic form. The other choices are ordinary multiplication, a wrong-sign integral, a frequency-domain statement, or an incorrectly truncated integral.

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression is the equivalent convolution-integral form of $y(t)=p(t)*q(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The convolution symbol $*$ expands to $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p(\tau)q(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, which is the standard time-domain form for an LTI output. The other choices are a product, the compact notation only, a wrong-sign integral, or a frequency-domain product.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Applying the Fourier Transform to the Convolution Equation

prompt_blocks.text: Starting from $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, which relation appears after applying $\mathcal{F}$ to both sides, before simplification?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the Fourier transform to both sides of the convolution equation. That changes the output to $Y(j\omega)$ but keeps the right-hand side symbolic for now.
The product $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ comes only after the convolution theorem is applied in the next step.

prompt_blocks.text: After applying $\mathcal{F}$ to the compact convolution equation $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, which relation appears before the convolution theorem is used?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The transform of the left-hand side is $Y(j\omega)$. Before the convolution theorem is named, the right-hand side stays as the transform of the convolution.
So the correct choice is the unsimplified transformed relation, not the product form that comes later.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Using the Convolution Theorem on the Output Spectrum

prompt_blocks.text: After applying the convolution theorem to $Y(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{x(t)*h(t)\}$, which expression should replace the transformed convolution?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The convolution theorem replaces the transformed convolution with the product of the two spectra. The frequency variable stays $j\omega$, so the simplified output relation is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)\,\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression is the frequency-domain product form of $\mathcal{F}\{x(t)*h(t)\}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The convolution theorem turns a convolution in time into a product in frequency. So $\mathcal{F}\{x(t)*h(t)\}$ becomes $X(j\omega)\,\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$, not a convolution or a sum.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output

prompt_blocks.text: What notation names the Fourier transform of the impulse response $h(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The impulse-response transform is written as $H(j\omega)$. This is the standard frequency-response notation, and it means $H(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$.

prompt_blocks.text: After replacing $\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$ with that notation, which equation is the correct output relation?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute the transform notation into the product form. The system term becomes $H(j\omega)$, so the output relation is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output

prompt_blocks.text: Which equation correctly completes the derivation after applying the Fourier transform to the LTI convolution equation and identifying $H(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The convolution theorem turns the transformed convolution into a product, and the definition $H(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$ names the system factor. So the completed output relation is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

prompt_blocks.text: After the Fourier transform and the convolution theorem are applied, which relation gives the LTI output spectrum in its final form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The transformed convolution is replaced by a product, not a sum or quotient. Since $H(j\omega)$ is the transform of the impulse response, the final relation is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
